articles.title: Dyadic: A Scalable Platform for Research on Human–Human and Human–AI Conversation
articles.authors: David M. Markowitz
articles.abstract: Conversation is ubiquitous in social life, but the empirical study of this interactive process has been thwarted by tools that are insufficiently modular and unadaptive to researcher needs. To relieve many constraints in conversation research, in the current tutorial, I present an overview and walkthrough of a new tool, Dyadic ( https://www.chatdyadic.com ), a web-based platform for studying human–human and human–artificial intelligence (AI) conversations using text-based or voice-based chats. Dyadic is distinct from other platforms by offering studies with multiple modalities, AI suggestions (e.g., in human–human studies, AI can suggest responses to a participant), live monitoring (e.g., researchers can evaluate chats between communicators in real time), and survey deployment (e.g., Likert-type scales, feeling thermometers, and open-ended text boxes can be sent to humans for in situ evaluations of the interaction), among other consequential features. No coding is required to operate Dyadic directly, and integrations with existing survey and participant-recruitment platforms are offered.

articles.title: How much habituation is enough? An R application for ad hoc content-related limits of acceptance in behavioral research
articles.authors: Konstantin Warneke, Stanislav D. Siegel, José Afonso, Marco Herbsleb, Sebastian Wallot
articles.abstract: Evaluating test–retest reliability is of crucial importance for clinical decision-making and an integral component of studies in empirical sciences. In psychology, classical test theory focused on reliability coefficients, but research has shown that intraclass correlation coefficients and Cronbach’s alpha have limited value in quantifying individual measurement error sources appropriately. Preliminary assumptions such as parallel readings and independency of error sources are violated by practice/habituation effects, i.e., test–retest systematic errors. Although awareness of the need for additional measurement quantifications to properly assess test–retest agreement has increased, many such quantifications are insufficiently implemented. Furthermore, one of the most important agreement analyses introduced by Bland and Altman in 1986 has interpretation limitations, as the limits of agreement are descriptive and not linked to content-based clinical decision-making, oftentimes causing inappropriate usage. To counteract these limitations and improve the implementation of agreement analyses in addition to more commonly used reliability coefficients, we introduce a software package that allows predefining acceptable measurement limits (limits of acceptance) to evaluate the sufficiency of task habituation to gauge individual error sources. The package implements a comprehensive test–retest evaluation in order to improve transparency of data quality reporting in psychological and cognitive research.

articles.title: Quantifying infants’ everyday restrained experiences in the home using wearable inertial sensors
articles.authors: Hanzhi Wang, Hailey N. Rousey, John M. Franchak
articles.abstract: Physical restraint—including being held, carried, and restrained in devices—is a common feature of infants’ everyday lives. However, previous survey-based and video-based methods cannot simultaneously provide continuous, full-day accounts of infants’ restrained experiences. This study developed and validated a machine learning model to quantify infants’ restrained time moment-to-moment across the full day in the home environment using wearable sensor data. We used a dataset that includes 146 home-visit sessions from 66 infants, with 30 younger infants aged 4–7 months, and 36 older infants aged 11–14 months. We annotated infants’ restrained states in the first 1.5-h video recording of each session as ground-truth labels. The supervised machine-learning model achieved high accuracy (89%) and substantial kappa agreement (κ = .73) compared with human-coded ground truth. The model showed a slight bias toward overestimating unrestrained periods relative to restrained periods, but this bias was mitigated when we used a longer data-aggregation window. The model also showed convergent validity by corroborating prior studies that showed an age-related decrease in infants’ overall restrained time throughout the day. In short, the current study demonstrated the utility of using wearable sensors to quantify infants’ real-world restrained experiences, offering a new tool for studying how daily restraint influences early development.

articles.title: VRrec: A zero-coding open-source VR body-motion capture tool for behavioral research
articles.authors: Pawel Kobylinski, Bartosz Muczynski, Daniel Cnotkowski, Mariusz Wierzbowski, Cezary Biele
articles.abstract: We present VRrec, an open-source, motion-tracking and recording tool for PC-based virtual reality (VR). The tool addresses a persistent gap in VR-based experimental research by enabling real-time capture of head, hand, and optional body-tracking data without the need to code. VRrec runs discreetly in the background, collecting positional and rotational data as researchers engage participants with third-party VR applications. This design lets researchers use flexible paradigms that leverage off-the-shelf VR content, eliminating the need to build or modify custom software. However, because VRrec does not read application-level events or object states from the target VR software, it does not directly support paradigms that require synchronization with in-app events or distances to dynamic virtual objects or avatars. VRrec still allows manual event marking for contextual annotation. The resulting data are stored as plain text, which can be imported into various analysis pipelines to derive behavioral metrics in fields such as social psychology, rehabilitation, and consumer research. Evaluations show consistent and stable recording performance with minimal impact on system resources, while also indicating some limitations for study designs that require millisecond-accurate timing precision. By streamlining VR motion data acquisition, VRrec broadens the range of feasible VR study designs and reduces technical barriers, making VR-based behavioral research more accessible. Both the source code and the executable version of VRrec are freely available on GitHub.

articles.title: Higher Perceived Inequalities Strengthen the Relationship between Economic Insecurity and Anti-Elite Attitudes
articles.authors: Nele Claes, Medhi Marot, Efrain Garcia-Sanchez, Toon Kuppens, Antony S. R. Manstead, Bram Spruyt, Alice Normand, Céline Darnon
articles.abstract: This research examined the psychological mechanisms underlying anti-elite attitudes, focusing on the roles of economic insecurity and perceived economic inequality. In a preregistered study using a large representative sample across nine European countries (Belgium, Denmark, France, Greece, Hungary, Netherlands, Poland, Spain, and the UK, N = 11,217), we investigated whether feelings of relative deprivation explain the association between perceived personal economic insecurity and two anti-elite attitudes (i.e., populist attitudes and distrust in institutions) and whether perceived societal economic inequality reinforces these effects. The results show that (i) the more individuals feel insecure about their economic situation, the more they report anti-elite attitudes, (ii) which is explained by a greater feeling of relative deprivation (between 43% and 59% of variance explained), (iii) and this relationship is stronger for individuals who perceive greater economic inequalities within their country. This research provides evidence that feelings of relative deprivation constitute an important psychological process underpinning anti-elite attitudes across diverse economic, cultural, and political contexts.

articles.title: Field Philosophy: A Methodological Approach to Organizational Philosophy-in-Practice
articles.authors: Stephanie Daher, Gazi Islam, Anahid Roux-Rosier
articles.abstract: Organizational research methods have increasingly been concerned with the relation between scholarship and practice, as part of an impact-oriented, responsible management literature. These concerns find an unexpected ally in recent developments within the field of philosophy, in which a distant and abstract relation to the field is replaced by a practice-oriented, collaboratively intense form of engagement referred to as “field philosophy.” Considered as an organizational research method, field philosophy emphasizes exchange, knowledge from below, and insider–outsider collaboration. The current article develops field philosophy for the study of organizational phenomena, illustrating this method with an empirical illustration from a field study of a carbon credit project in the Brazilian Amazon, and drawing out implications for the design and application of field philosophical methods for studying organizations.

articles.title: Grateful for What and Whom? How Gratitude List Content Varies and Is Associated With Affective Responses
articles.authors: Yoobin Park, Elissa S. Epel, Emiliana Simon-Thomas
articles.abstract: A gratitude list activity, whereby one recalls and writes down things they are grateful for, is a well-studied intervention known to confer an immediate and even prolonged boost in well-being. However, the specific content people reflect on, and how it relates to affective evaluations and the impact of the intervention, remains underexplored. Using data from a global online study ( N = 19,265), we applied natural language processing to examine the content of gratitude lists, identifying 16 thematic clusters, with the most common one focused on social relationships. Next, we examined and found various sociodemographic and psychological differences in people’s gratitude list content. Further, mentioning themes related to family or nature was associated with greater increases in positivity following the activity. Overall, our findings highlight individual differences in what people naturally think of during this popular intervention and suggest opportunities for personalized modifications to enhance adherence to and effectiveness of the intervention.

articles.title: A Safe Town? Ostensible State or County Racial Climate Impacts Perceptions of Town-Level Racial Identity-Safety Cues
articles.authors: Izilda Pereira-Jorge, Kim E. Chaney
articles.abstract: Identity-safety cues (ISCs) are environmental signals that indicate one’s marginalized identity is valued. ISC contextual information may impact town evaluations. Over three experiments ( N = 1,107), we examine how single or multiple ISCs posted across storefronts (i.e., Black lives matter flag, Study 1–3) and the racial climate surrounding a hypothetical town (Study 2–3) impact attributions of ISC motives and town evaluations. Racial minorities and Black Americans perceived greater external diversity motives (e.g., social pressure) of a storefront with an ISC when all other storefronts had an ISC compared to when no other storefronts had an ISC (Study 1–3). Ostensible state- and county-level racially egalitarian climates elicited greater expectations of internal diversity motives and positive town evaluations (e.g., greater progressive policies, quality of life, Black residents) compared to prejudicial racial climates and towns with a single ISC (Study 2–3). Findings demonstrate the need to consider multiple levels of ISCs.

articles.title: Psychometric Properties of the Turkish Version of the Musical Activity and Well-Being Scale: A Methodological Study From Türkiye
articles.authors: Buket Şimşek Arslan, Alper Börekci
articles.abstract: This study aimed to examine the validity and reliability of the Turkish version of the Musical Activity and Well-Being Scale. This methodological study was conducted with 424 adults engaged in musical activities at either amateur or professional levels. Following the World Health Organization’s translation and back-translation protocol, the scale was adapted into Turkish and evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency analyses, and correlations with related measures. The findings supported the original five-factor structure of the scale and provided evidence for construct validity. Internal consistency analysis indicated excellent overall reliability (α = .93). In addition, meaningful relationships with measures of musical impact and psychological well-being offered further support for validity. Overall, the results suggest that the Turkish version of the Musical Activity and Well-Being Scale is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing music-related well-being. The scale provides a valuable tool for research and practice in music psychology, education, and health contexts.
